summary:
The Republic of the Congo does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct between adults. A systematic legislative review in the EUAA May 2024 Query Response Q29 reached that finding, and the United States Department of State human rights reports for 2022 and 2023 record the same position. Same-sex relationships have been legal since 1940.

Penal Code Article 331, as amended in 2006, imposes an unequal age of consent of 21 years for same-sex acts compared with 18 years for different-sex acts. It punishes shameless acts or acts against nature with a person of the same sex under 21 with six months to three years imprisonment and a fine. The EUAA review and the Department of State reports describe the scope of that provision as applied to same-sex conduct as ambiguous, with sources treating it as a basis to justify discrimination.

The provision has not been used for formal prosecution in the reporting period. The 2022 Department of State report states it was not invoked for prosecutions. The 2023 report records no known arrests or prosecutions of LGBTQI+ persons under it during 2023.

Police use the provision in street-level encounters to obtain money. The 2022 report states police at times cited it to extract bribes from gay men. The 2023 report states police continued to use the act against nature law as a pretext to solicit bribes from men. A separate account states police have solicited bribes from young men perceived as gay and have falsely claimed that same-sex activity is generally illegal for that purpose. Such abuses are rarely reported because of fear of police contact, but are investigated when reported.

Local nongovernmental organizations reported violence, psychological and physical harassment, and financial extortion of LGBTQI+ persons by government actors and nonstate actors. The 2023 report describes that pattern as continuing.

The law provides no anti-discrimination protection on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. There are no hate-crime provisions. There are no provisions addressing discrimination in education, healthcare, housing or employment.

There is no legally recognized procedure to change gender identity.

Same-sex marriage is explicitly excluded. Section 2, Article 127 of the Family Code defines marriage as a public act establishing a lasting union between a man and a woman.

Societal hostility is high. In a survey conducted from 2021 to 2023, 73 percent of people in Brazzaville said they would dislike or strongly dislike having a homosexual neighbour. State authorities and ordinary citizens committed violence against LGBTQ+ people in 2022 and 2023. Reported violence against LGBTQ people is punished by law enforcement.

LGBTQ civil society organizations were present in 2023 but had been unable to obtain legal recognition. In 2020 one nongovernmental organization was denied registration until references to its focus on the LGBTQ+ community were removed.
tangentialFactors:
Violence against LGBTQ+ people increased in 2022 in conditions of forced confinement during the COVID-19 pandemic. Increasing economic hardship contributed further. Most of that violence was committed by family members.

Personal-data rules protect information about sexual orientation and sexual life but not gender identity. Article 19 of Law No. 27-2020 on the Fight against Cybercrime prohibits placing or storing personal data revealing sexual orientation without a legal exception or express consent, punishable by one to five years in prison, a fine of one million to ten million CFA francs, or both. Articles 8, 10 and 15 of Decree No. 2025-66 on the personal data of air passengers protect sexual orientation, and Articles 4, 14 and 40 of Law No. 29-2019 on the Protection of Personal Data protect sexual life as sensitive and personal data.
localsOnly: The law does not address conversion therapy. It does not address surgeries on intersex children intended to make their bodies conform to expected norms.
outOfScopeNotes: Trans-specific societal tolerance is unresolved. The sources contain no documented statement about tolerance of transgender people specifically. All tolerance and violence findings are framed around LGBTQ people generally or homosexual neighbours.
